How fast have energy transitions happened before? – Honglin Li

# How fast have energy transitions happened before?

Overlay a century of U.S. adoption curves, from electric service in homes to solar’s share of electricity, and see what sped some up and held others back

 X3 of Energy Systems, Step by Step: read a century of U.S. adoption curves, from electricity in homes to solar’s share of electricity, and say how fast each change moved and why, from dated sources and with no forecast. 

U.S. adoption curves, as shares over time (each from a dated source)

| Curve | First point | Last point | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Homes with electric service | 8.0% in 1907 | 98.8% in 1956 | Census Bureau, Historical Statistics (1975), Series S 109-111 |
| Town and other non-farm homes with electric service | 47.4% in 1920 | 99.2% in 1956 | Census Bureau, Historical Statistics (1975), Series S 109-111 |
| Farm homes with electric service | 1.6% in 1920 | 95.9% in 1956 | Census Bureau, Historical Statistics (1975), Series S 109-111 |
| Homes heated mainly with piped gas | 11.3% in 1940 | 51.2% in 2000 | Census Bureau, House Heating Fuel, 1940-2000 |
| Homes heated mainly with coal or coke | 54.7% in 1940 | 0.1% in 2000 | Census Bureau, House Heating Fuel, 1940-2000 |
| Families owning a car | 54.0% in 1948 | 82.0% in 1970 | Census Bureau, Historical Statistics (1975), Series Q 153 and Q 175 |
| Solar's share of U.S. electricity | 1.0% in 2015 | 8.7% in 2025 | EIA, Electric Power Annual, Table 3.1.A |

Every plotted point, with what each curve counts

| Curve | Points (year: share) | What is counted | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Homes with electric service | 1907: 8.0%; 1912: 15.9%; 1917: 24.3%; 1920: 34.7%; 1925: 53.2%; 1930: 68.2%; 1935: 68.0%; 1940: 78.7%; 1945: 85.0%; 1950: 94.0%; 1955: 98.4%; 1956: 98.8% | the share of all homes (dwelling units) with electric service | Census Bureau, Historical Statistics (1975), Series S 109-111, Series S 109 |
| Town and other non-farm homes with electric service | 1920: 47.4%; 1925: 69.4%; 1930: 84.8%; 1935: 83.9%; 1940: 90.8%; 1945: 93.0%; 1950: 96.6%; 1955: 98.8%; 1956: 99.2% | the share of town and other non-farm homes (urban and rural non-farm dwelling units) with electric service | Census Bureau, Historical Statistics (1975), Series S 109-111, Series S 111 |
| Farm homes with electric service | 1920: 1.6%; 1925: 3.9%; 1930: 10.4%; 1935: 12.6%; 1940: 32.6%; 1945: 48.0%; 1950: 77.7%; 1955: 94.4%; 1956: 95.9% | the share of farm homes (farm dwelling units) with electric service | Census Bureau, Historical Statistics (1975), Series S 109-111, Series S 110 |
| Homes heated mainly with piped gas | 1940: 11.3%; 1950: 26.6%; 1960: 43.1%; 1970: 55.2%; 1980: 53.1%; 1990: 51.0%; 2000: 51.2% | the share of occupied homes heated mainly with piped gas (the census's utility gas); the 1940 figure also counts bottled gas, so 1940 is not like for like | Census Bureau, House Heating Fuel, 1940-2000, national rows, 1940 to 2000 |
| Homes heated mainly with coal or coke | 1940: 54.7%; 1950: 34.6%; 1960: 12.2%; 1970: 2.9%; 1980: 0.6%; 1990: 0.4%; 2000: 0.1% | the share of occupied homes heated mainly with coal or coke (a fuel made by baking coal) | Census Bureau, House Heating Fuel, 1940-2000, national rows, 1940 to 2000 |
| Families owning a car | 1948: 54.0%; 1950: 59.0%; 1955: 70.0%; 1960: 77.0%; 1965: 79.0%; 1970: 82.0% | the share of families owning at least one car, from a household survey that began in 1947; Alaska and Hawaii are left out | Census Bureau, Historical Statistics (1975), Series Q 153 and Q 175, Series Q 175 |
| Solar's share of U.S. electricity | 2015: 1.0%; 2017: 1.9%; 2019: 2.6%; 2021: 4.0%; 2023: 5.6%; 2025: 8.7% | solar generation from utility-scale plants (1 MW or larger) and from small systems, including rooftop panels, as a share of all U.S. generation (our arithmetic on EIA's table) | EIA, Electric Power Annual, Table 3.1.A, Table 3.1.A, 2015 to 2025 |

- Town and other non-farm homes passed half between 1920 and 1925; farm homes between 1945 and 1950, about 25 years later.
- Coal heated 34.6% of homes in 1950 and piped gas 43.1% in 1960. Gas overtook coal as the most common main heating fuel between the 1950 and 1960 censuses.
- Other fuels, such as heating oil, changed too; these census snapshots do not track homes switching from one fuel to another.
- Families owning a car: 54% in 1948, 82% in 1970. Registered cars rose from 0.46 million in 1910 to 23.0 million in 1930.
- Solar made 1.0% of U.S. electricity in 2015 and 8.7% in 2025, counting small systems such as rooftop panels (our arithmetic on EIA's table).

Real numbers, as published: each point comes from a dated U.S. source, the Census Bureau (Historical Statistics, 1975; housing censuses) or EIA. Solar's share is our arithmetic on EIA's table.

## What you just did, as diagrams

Decades, not years
: On its diffusion curve, electric service went from 8% of U.S. homes in 1907 to over 90% between 1945 and 1950.
Not everywhere at once
: Farms passed half about 25 years after town homes; wires had to reach them first.
Gas overtook coal
: Piped gas overtook coal as the most common main heating fuel between the 1950 and 1960 censuses. Other fuels changed too; the snapshots do not track homes switching.
What sped it
: Networks built and public programs sped U.S. curves up; in British history, cheaper or better services drove change, and refining a new source took decades.
Say what you measure
: A device in homes, a fuel's share of a nation and a share of electricity move at different speeds.

U.S. energy transitions, dated

1. 1850 · Coal at 9% of U.S. energy. Coal supplied 9% of U.S. energy use, and 27% by 1870 as railroads spread. Source: EIA, Today in Energy, 30 June 2026
2. 1882 · Pearl Street Station. One of the world's first central power plants opened in New York; it could power 5,000 lights. Source: EIA, Energy Kids, electricity timeline
3. 1885 · Coal passes wood. Around 1885 coal passed wood as the largest U.S. energy source. Source: EIA, Today in Energy, 30 June 2026
4. 1907 · 8% of homes have electric service. The first year of the Census Bureau's series of homes with electric service. Source: Census Bureau, Historical Statistics (1975), Series S 109-111
5. 1908 · Model T. Ford first produced the Model T car. Source: EIA, Energy Kids, transportation timeline
6. 1936 · Rural Electrification Act. A law aimed at bringing electricity to farms across the country. Source: EIA, Energy Kids, electricity timeline
7. 1950 · Petroleum passes coal. Petroleum became the most-used U.S. energy source, and has been ever since. Source: EIA, Today in Energy, 30 June 2026
8. 1956 · Interstate Highway System. The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 established the Interstate Highway System. Source: EIA, Energy Kids, transportation timeline
9. 1958 · Natural gas passes coal. Natural gas passed coal in U.S. energy use; it has been second most years since. Source: EIA, Today in Energy, 2 July 2025
10. 1970 · Gas heats most homes. Piped gas heated 55.2% of homes and coal or coke 2.9%, against 11.3% (with bottled gas) and 54.7% in 1940. Source: Census Bureau, House Heating Fuel, 1940-2000
11. 2023 · Renewables pass coal. U.S. energy use from renewables passed coal for the first time since the 1880s. Source: EIA, Today in Energy, 30 June 2026
12. 2025 · Solar at 8.7% of electricity. Solar made 8.7% of U.S. electricity, large plants and small systems together (our arithmetic). Source: EIA, Electric Power Annual, Table 3.1.A

### This side topic stops at reading the curves

Adoption enters the course only as diffusion, a share over time; costs and forecasts stay out.

#### This side topic covers

- What share of homes, families or electricity each change reached, and when.
- What sped some curves up and held others back, read from dated sources.
- Why the answer to 'how fast' depends on what you measure.

#### Left to specialists

- How the cost of any technology changed over time.
- Forecasts of how fast anything spreads next.
- Economic history beyond these curves: prices, wages, trade.

#### Read next, three rungs

1. Start here. Long-run charts of the world's energy sources, with how each series is built. Our World in Data, Energy: Energy Sources and Transitions (Ritchie, Rosado and Roser), published 20 December 2023, read 7 November 2026
2. Go further. How long national and global transitions took, country by country. Vaclav Smil, Energy Transitions: Global and National Perspectives (Praeger), cited by name, second edition, 2017
3. Go deep. Energy across human history, from muscle power to fossil fuels and electricity. Vaclav Smil, Energy and Civilization: A History (MIT Press), cited by name, 2017

Go deeper · Analyst Reading a diffusion curve without fooling yourself

- Say the whole. A share of homes, of families and of electricity are three different wholes; a curve means nothing until its denominator is named.
- Published points only. The page reports a year as “between 1945 and 1950” rather than drawing a smooth line through gaps.
- Starts and ends. The car survey began when most families already had a car; solar’s curve stops at the latest year of data.
- Services first. Grubler (2012, abstract) points to energy end use and services, and to the lengthy process of transitions.

## Check yourself

About a minute: two myths.

Myth or fact? “Farm homes and town homes passed half with electric service at about the same time.”

Answer

Myth. Town and other non-farm homes passed half between 1920 and 1925; farm homes only between 1945 and 1950, about 25 years later (Census Bureau).

Myth or fact? “Petroleum has been the largest source of U.S. energy since 1950.”

Answer

Fact. Petroleum passed coal in 1950; coal had passed wood around 1885 (EIA, 2026).
